concepts.note: Dark lines arise when cooler solar gases absorb specific wavelengths from the continuous photosphere.
concepts.title: Solar absorption spectrum

concepts.note: The prominent D lines near 589 nm were later identified with sodium.
concepts.title: Fraunhofer D lines

concepts.note: Fraunhofer's gratings enabled accurate measurement of spectral line wavelengths.
concepts.title: Diffraction grating

concepts.note: Each chemical element has a unique emission and absorption spectrum, founding analytical spectroscopy.
concepts.title: Kirchhoff–Bunsen law

subtopics.note: Fraunhofer mapped the dark absorption lines of the solar spectrum and labeled the principal ones, turning spectroscopy into a precision probe of matter. Kirchhoff and Bunsen later explained in 1859 that each element produces a characteristic set of lines.
subtopics.title: Fraunhofer lines

concepts.note: The formula predicts the wavelengths of the visible hydrogen series from a simple integer relation.
concepts.title: Balmer formula

concepts.note: The n = 3 to n = 2 transition gives the red H-alpha line at 656.3 nm.
concepts.title: H-alpha line

concepts.note: Rydberg generalized the pattern to 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) for all hydrogen series.
concepts.title: Rydberg formula

concepts.note: Bohr's quantized angular momentum L = nħ reproduced the Balmer formula and introduced atomic energy levels.
concepts.title: Bohr explanation

subtopics.note: Balmer found an empirical formula fitting the visible hydrogen lines, 1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/n²) for n = 3, 4, ..., with R the Rydberg constant. Bohr derived it in 1913 from quantized electron orbits.
subtopics.title: Balmer series

concepts.note: The normal pattern has frequency shifts Δν = 0, ±eB/(4πmₑ), equivalent to energy shifts ΔE = μB B m_l.
concepts.title: Normal Zeeman triplet

concepts.note: Many lines split into patterns not explained classically, pointing to spin and angular-momentum coupling.
concepts.title: Anomalous Zeeman effect

concepts.note: The g-factor parametrizes the magnetic moment of a coupled atomic state.
concepts.title: Landé g-factor

concepts.note: The emitted components have polarizations fixed by the change in magnetic quantum number.
concepts.title: Polarization selection rules

subtopics.note: Zeeman observed that magnetic fields split spectral lines, and Lorentz explained the normal triplet using classical electron oscillators. The anomalous Zeeman effect later required electron spin and the Landé g-factor.
subtopics.title: Zeeman effect

concepts.note: A₂₁ gives spontaneous emission, while B₁₂ and B₂₁ give absorption and stimulated emission rates.
concepts.title: A and B coefficients

concepts.note: The emitted photon has the same frequency, phase, and direction as the stimulating photon.
concepts.title: Stimulated photon amplification

concepts.note: A nonequilibrium state with more atoms in the upper level is needed for net stimulated amplification.
concepts.title: Population inversion

concepts.note: Detailed balance gives A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³ and B₁₂ = B₂₁ for nondegenerate levels.
concepts.title: Einstein relations

subtopics.note: Einstein introduced spontaneous and stimulated emission through A and B coefficients, showing that an incident photon can trigger emission of an identical photon. This process is the basis of masers and lasers.
subtopics.title: Stimulated emission

concepts.note: The Cs-133 ground-state hyperfine splitting provides a stable, reproducible frequency standard.
concepts.title: Caesium hyperfine transition

concepts.note: Two separated microwave interactions produce a narrow interference fringe used to lock the clock.
concepts.title: Ramsey separated fields

concepts.note: The SI second is defined by ν = ΔE/h = 9,192,631,770 Hz for the Cs-133 hyperfine transition.
concepts.title: SI second definition

subtopics.note: Essen and Parry built the first practical caesium-beam atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory, locking an oscillator to the Cs-133 hyperfine transition. The 1967 SI second was defined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of that transition.
subtopics.title: Atomic clock

concepts.note: Maiman's ruby laser emitted at 694.3 nm and established the laser as a practical device.
concepts.title: Ruby laser

concepts.note: Optical pumping creates more atoms in the upper laser level than the lower level.
concepts.title: Population inversion

concepts.note: Mirrors provide feedback and select longitudinal and transverse modes.
concepts.title: Optical resonator

concepts.note: Oscillation starts when round-trip gain exceeds loss, approximately R₁R₂ exp(2gL) ≥ 1.
concepts.title: Laser threshold

subtopics.note: Maiman demonstrated the first laser, a flashlamp-pumped ruby rod, in 1960, using stimulated emission in a population-inverted medium. Schawlow and Townes had proposed the optical maser/laser concept in 1958.
subtopics.title: Laser

concepts.note: The JILA experiment cooled Rb-87 atoms in a magnetic trap to nanokelvin temperatures.
concepts.title: Rubidium-87 condensate

concepts.note: Ketterle's MIT group achieved BEC in sodium and observed matter-wave interference.
concepts.title: Sodium condensate

concepts.note: The condensate is described by a single complex order parameter with coherent phase.
concepts.title: Macroscopic wavefunction

concepts.note: Mean-field theory gives iħ∂ψ/∂t = (−ħ²/2m ∇² + V + g|ψ|²)ψ.
concepts.title: Gross-Pitaevskii equation

subtopics.note: Predicted by Bose and Einstein in 1924–25, a BEC was first realized in dilute atomic gases by Cornell and Wieman in rubidium-87 at JILA in 1995, followed by Ketterle's sodium condensate at MIT. Below a critical temperature, bosons macroscopically occupy the same quantum state.
subtopics.title: Bose-Einstein condensate
